newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens say Russians behind Red Cross killings.
newsitem.headline: Chechens say Russians behind Red Cross killings.

text.p: Chechnya's separatist government said on Thursday elements in the Russian security forces were behind a string of recent killings in the rebel region including the murder of six Red Cross workers.

"The structures of the Russian special forces and the Federal Security Service are engaged in financing and preparing terrorist acts on Chechen territory," separatist government spokesman Movladi Udugov told Reuters.
Six foreign workers from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) were shot dead at a hospital on Tuesday, prompting the agency to pull out of Chechnya.
Udugov, who holds the rank of deputy prime minister, said Russian forces were also behind the shooting of six local people -- mostly ethnic Russians -- in the capital Grozny on Wednesday.
He said the murders were carried out by hired Chechen killers and added that the Chechen government did not believe the Russian leadership was aware of these activities.

"The events of the past few days...demonstrate that the anti-Chechen war is not over," Udugov said. "The dirtiest, most perfidious methods are being used, which the organisers intend should completely deprive the Chechen people of the support of the world community and Russian society.
"Chechnya is to play the role of a criminal cesspool, which should be isolated from the rest of the world."
The Kremlin had no immediate comment on the allegation.
No one has claimed responsibility for this week's murders, the most dramatic in a series of violent incidents that have heightened tensions in the region.
Maverick rebel commander Salman Raduyev, an Islamic hardliner, captured 22 policemen at the weekend but freed them on Wednesday under pressure from the separatist leadership.
When President Boris Yeltsin sent troops into Chechnya in December 1994, he quoted a need to rein in the breakaway region and described it as a "safe haven" for criminals from across Russia.
Under an August 31 peace deal, Russia is withdrawing troops from Chechnya and leaving it under full separatist control.
All notable rebel figures, including Udugov, have announced plans to run for president in elections scheduled for January 27. Voters will also be electing a new local parliament.

Chechen leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who hopes the vote will confirm him in his currently unelected post of president, underwent an operation on Wednesday on an arm broken in a car accident last week, Interfax news agency said.
It said Yandarbiyev would soon be back at work.
Opponents of the peace deal in the Russian parliament say it has taken things back to square one and demand that Chechnya be sealed off from the rest of the country.
Wednesday's killing of six people in Grozny's southern suburbs frightened many ethnic Russians and prompted them to leave or make plans to leave, local residents said.
Residents of the neighbourhood in Grozny's southern suburbs where six people were killed on Wednesday said ethnic Russians were scared and many were leaving or making plans to do so.
Three men and two women were shot dead in a flat and a sixth, a man, nearby. "We're suffering. We have to get away," said Tamara Bunyayeva, a friend of one of the women.
Up to a third of Chechnya's prewar population of one million were Russians. Many fled the fighting. "We'd leave too but we can't afford it and we've nowhere else to go," Bunyayeva said.
The authorities in Grozny acknowledge that ethnic Russians are more frequent victims of criminal attacks than Chechens. But they insist they do not wish to force Russians out of Chechnya.
They say that Russians, who are not protected by powerful family clans, are simply easier target for bandits.
